The three major festivals are in boldFestivals according to the shrine history.. * Monthly ** Monthly Festival (1st, 5th, 28th) ** Usagi Day Festival (Usagi Day) * January ** New Year's Festival (January 1) ** Rice Planting Festival (January 5) ** New Year's Festival (January 15) * February ** Setsubun Festival (Setsubun Day in February) ** National Foundation Day Festival (February 11) * March ** '''Prayer Festival''' (March 15) ** First Usagi Lecture Festival (Old Calendar February Usagi Day) * April ** Higime Lecture Society Festival (Mid-April) ** Spring Festival (April 28) * June ** Great Purification Ceremony (June 30) * July ** Kashiwa Festival (July 15) * September ** Yaejime Festival (September 1) ** Mid-Autumn Festival (September 14) ** '''Grand Festival''' (September 15) ** Autumn Festival (September 24) * November ** Meiji Day Festival (November 3) * December ** Kama Purification Ritual (December 3) ** '''Grand Head Festival (New Harvest Festival)''' (December 10-14) ** Emperor's Birthday Festival (December 23) ** Great Purification Ceremony, New Year's Eve Festival (December 31)
=== Grand Head Festival === The Grand Head Festival (Niinamesai) held from December 10 to 14 is called the "Daitōsai". The festival is led by five headmen, with the third headman being called "Daitō," giving the festival its name. The "Headman's Record" (御頭帳) traces back to Bunroku 1 (1592), making it a festival with a history of over 400 years. It is a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} ({{ill|Myojin Taisha|ja|名神大}}) and the fourth shrine of {{ill|Shinano Province|ja|信濃国}}. It was formerly classified as a {{ill|Prefectural shrine|ja|県社}} and is now a {{ill|Beppyo Shrine|ja|別表神社}} under the Association of Shinto Shrines. The shrine's old name was "Hachiman Shrine," and it is still commonly referred to as "Yawata-sama" or "Yawata Shrine." == deity == '''Main deity''' * '''{{ill|Takemizuwake no Ōkami|ja|武美名別命}}''' (Takemizuwake no Ōkami)According to the shrine's history. *: The shrine's tradition states that this deity was enshrined to pray for the fertility of the Zenkoji Plain and to prevent the flooding of the Chikuma River. '''Deities in the Same Shrine''' : The three deities enshrined together here collectively represent the {{ill|Hachiman deity|ja|八幡神}}. * Hondawake no Mikoto (誉田別命, {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|ja|応神天皇}}) * Okinagatarashihime no Mikoto (息長足比売命, {{ill|Empress Jingū|ja|神功皇后}}) * Hime Ōkami (比咩大神) == History == === Overview === According to shrine tradition, it was established during the reign of the 8th Emperor {{ill|Emperor Kōgen|ja|孝元天皇}}Shrine history.. The earliest record in historical documents is from {{ill|Jogan|ja|貞観}} 8 (866), when it was given the rank of {{ill|Junior Second rank|ja|従二位}} from no rank. Additionally, it is listed as "Takemizuwake Shrine" in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}} compiled in {{ill|Engi|ja|延長}} 5 (927), categorized as a {{ill|Myojin Taisha|ja|名神大}}. However, the evidence supporting the identification of this shrine as the one mentioned in the documents is not definitive『日本の神々』 Takemizuwake Shrine entry., and another candidate is {{ill|Okeno Omi Shrine|ja|桶知大神社}} in Nagano City. The area around Takemizuwake Shrine became an estate ({{ill|Shōen|ja|荘園}}) of {{ill|Iwashimizu Hachiman Shrine|ja|石清水八幡宮}} (Otani estate) from the late Heian period, and it is said that the Hachiman deity (the three deities enshrined together) was invited from Iwashimizu Hachiman Shrine during the Anwa era (968-970). The Hachiman deity is known as the tutelary deity of the {{ill|Minamoto clan|ja|源氏}}, and Takemizuwake Shrine was widely revered by warriors as the foremost Hachiman Shrine in the region. It is also said that {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshinaka|ja|源義仲}} prayed here『参考源平盛衰記』 mentions on June 25 (or 14), Yōwa 1 (1181), that "八幡社ヲ伏拝ミ". However, it is unclear if this "Hachiman Shrine" is the same as Takemizuwake Shrine.. In {{ill|Hōgen|ja|保元}} 3 (1158), there is a record of lands in Otani estate, Sarashina District being confiscated by multiple officials. On that day, a government order was issued to halt thisIwashimizu document. During the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}} (1335), the Four Shrine clan, who served as Shinto priests of Takemizuwake Shrine, together with the Hoshina and Sekiya clans, attacked the {{ill|Shugo|ja|守護所}} (provincial headquarters) in Funeiyama (Suwa), but were suppressed. This resulted in the downfall of the Four Shrine clan, who were said to have served as both {{ill|Jitō|ja|地頭}} and district officials during their peak. The shrine buildings were burned down and later rebuilt at their current location. In {{ill|Tenshō|ja|天正}} 3 (1575), {{ill|Uesugi Kenshin|ja|上杉謙信}} offered a prayer document to the shrine, praying for victory against {{ill|Hōjō Ujizane|ja|北条氏政}}{{ill|Uesugi Kenshin prayer document|ja|上杉謙信願文集}}. In {{ill|Kanei|ja|寛永}} 1 (1624), the Tokugawa shogunate granted 200 koku of shrine land to the shrine. In Meiji 1 (1868), following the separation of Shinto and Buddhism ({{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|ja|神仏分離}}), the shrine was renamed "Takemizuwake Shrine" from "Hachiman Shrine," reflecting the disbanding of the associated temple ({{ill|Shinano Five Mountains|ja|信濃五山}}). The shrine was initially classified as a village shrine ({{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}) in the Modern Shrine ranking System but was promoted to a prefectural shrine ({{ill|Kensha|ja|県社}}) in Meiji 41 (1908). In 1876, the traditional Buddhist ceremony, the Grand Head festival ({{ill|Daitōsai|ja|大頭祭}}), was transformed into a Shinto ritual吉永みち子『もっと馬を!』平凡社、1990年、8 - 20ページ「木曽馬の村」. === Shrine ranks === * Jogan 8 (866) June, promoted from no rank to Junior Second rank (『{{ill|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|ja|日本三代実録}}』) * Jogan 9 (867) March 26, listed as a government shrine (『日本三代実録』) == Shrine Grounds == [[File:Takemizuwake-jinja honden.JPG|thumb|210px|right|{{center|Honden}}]] [[File:Takemizuwake-jinja keidai.JPG|thumb|210px|right|{{center|Shrine Grove (Nagano Prefecture designated natural monument)}}]] The shrine grounds cover 18,896 square meters and include a grove primarily composed of zelkova and cedar trees, with over 20 species and 400 trees in total. Many of the trees are old, and the "Takemizuwake Shrine Grove" is designated as a natural monument by Nagano Prefecture. The grounds, measuring approximately 280 meters from north to south and 70 meters from east to west, were originally square but were eroded into their current rectangular shape by frequent floods from the Chikuma River. A document from the Kanei era (1624-1644) was recently discovered, showing a square layout. Most of the current shrine buildings were constructed after a fire in Tenpō 13 (1842). The main hall was completed in Kaei 3 (1850) by Tatekawa Washiro II from Suwa. The worship hall was completed in Ansei 3 (1856) by Mineura Yagorō under Tatekawa Washiro's supervision. The main hall of the subsidiary Kōra Shrine is the oldest building, having survived the fire. The associated temple, known as Sarashina Hachiman Jinguji, was one of the Shinano Five Mountains of the Tendai sect but was abolished during the Meiji period's anti-Buddhist movement ({{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|ja|廃仏毀釈}}). == Subsidiary Shrines == === Subsidiary Shrines === [[File:Takemizuwake-jinja Kora-sha.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{center|Kōra Shrine}}{{small|The main hall inside the covering structure is a Nagano Prefecture treasure.}}]] * Kōra Shrine (高良社) *: The main hall inside the covering structure is the oldest in the shrine grounds, believed to have been built in the late Muromachi period (16th century). Particularly notable are the three major festivals: the Prayer festival (March 15), the Grand festival (September 15), and the Grand Head festival (New Harvest festival, December 10-14).

=== Grand Head festival === The Grand Head festival (Niinamesai) held from December 10 to 14 is called the "Daitōsai". The festival is led by five headmen, with the third headman being called "Daitō," giving the festival its name. The "Headman's Record" (御頭帳) traces back to Bunroku 1 (1592), making it a festival with a history of over 400 years. {{Infobox religious building| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Takemizuwake Shrine | image = Takemizuwake-jinja shaden.JPG |caption = From right: Chokushiden, Haiden, Honden | location = {{ill|Chikuma, Nagano|ja|千曲市}}, Nagano Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{coord|36|31|10.08|N|138|06|10.71|E|region:JP-20_type:landmark|display=inline,title|name=Takemizuwake Shrine}} | deity = {{ill|Takemizuwake no Ōkami|ja|武美名別命}} | object = | rank = {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} ({{ill|Myojin Taisha|ja|名神大}})
Fourth shrine of {{ill|Shinano Province|ja|信濃国}}
Former {{ill|Prefectural shrine|ja|県社}}
{{ill|Beppyo Shrine|ja|別表神社}} | established = During the reign of the 8th Emperor {{ill|Emperor Kōgen|ja|孝元天皇}} (trad.) | architecture = Nagare-zukuri | nickname = Hachiman Shrine | pilgrimage = | festival = September 15 | rituals = Daitōsai (Niinamesai), December 10-14 | map = Japan Nagano Prefecture | label = Takemizuwake Shrine | relief = 1 | map_width = 256 }} [[File:Takemizuwake-jinja ootorii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{center|Ōtorii}}]] '''Takemizuwake Shrine''' (武水別神社[[ja:武水別神社]]) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Chikuma, Nagano|ja|千曲市}}, Nagano Prefecture, Japan. It is a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} ({{ill|Myojin Taisha|ja|名神大}}) and the fourth shrine of {{ill|Shinano Province|ja|信濃国}}. It was formerly classified as a {{ill|Prefectural shrine|ja|県社}} and is now a {{ill|Beppyo Shrine|ja|別表神社}} under the Association of Shinto Shrines. The shrine's old name was "Hachiman Shrine," and it is still commonly referred to as "Yawata-sama" or "Yawata Shrine." == deity == '''Main deity''' * '''{{ill|Takemizuwake no Ōkami|ja|武美名別命}}''' (Takemizuwake no Ōkami)According to the shrine's history. *: The shrine's tradition states that this deity was enshrined to pray for the fertility of the Zenkoji Plain and to prevent the flooding of the Chikuma River. '''Deities in the Same Shrine''' : The three deities enshrined together here collectively represent the {{ill|Hachiman deity|ja|八幡神}}. * Hondawake no Mikoto (誉田別命, {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|ja|応神天皇}}) * Okinagatarashihime no Mikoto (息長足比売命, {{ill|Empress Jingū|ja|神功皇后}}) * Hime Ōkami (比咩大神) == History == === Overview === According to shrine tradition, it was established during the reign of the 8th Emperor {{ill|Emperor Kōgen|ja|孝元天皇}}Shrine history.. The earliest record in historical documents is from {{ill|Jogan|ja|貞観}} 8 (866), when it was given the rank of {{ill|Junior Second rank|ja|従二位}} from no rank. Additionally, it is listed as "Takemizuwake Shrine" in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}} compiled in {{ill|Engi|ja|延長}} 5 (927), categorized as a {{ill|Myojin Taisha|ja|名神大}}. However, the evidence supporting the identification of this shrine as the one mentioned in the documents is not definitive『日本の神々』 Takemizuwake Shrine entry., and another candidate is {{ill|Okeno Omi Shrine|ja|桶知大神社}} in Nagano City. The area around Takemizuwake Shrine became an estate ({{ill|Shōen|ja|荘園}}) of {{ill|Iwashimizu Hachiman Shrine|ja|石清水八幡宮}} (Otani estate) from the late Heian period, and it is said that the Hachiman deity (the three deities enshrined together) was invited from Iwashimizu Hachiman Shrine during the Anwa era (968-970). The Hachiman deity is known as the tutelary deity of the {{ill|Minamoto clan|ja|源氏}}, and Takemizuwake Shrine was widely revered by warriors as the foremost Hachiman Shrine in the region. It is also said that {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshinaka|ja|源義仲}} prayed here『参考源平盛衰記』 mentions on June 25 (or 14), Yōwa 1 (1181), that "八幡社ヲ伏拝ミ". However, it is unclear if this "Hachiman Shrine" is the same as Takemizuwake Shrine.. In {{ill|Hōgen|ja|保元}} 3 (1158), there is a record of lands in Otani estate, Sarashina District being confiscated by multiple officials. On that day, a government order was issued to halt thisIwashimizu document. During the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}} (1335), the Four Shrine clan, who served as Shinto priests of Takemizuwake Shrine, together with the Hoshina and Sekiya clans, attacked the {{ill|Shugo|ja|守護所}} (provincial headquarters) in Funeiyama (Suwa), but were suppressed. This resulted in the downfall of the Four Shrine clan, who were said to have served as both {{ill|Jitō|ja|地頭}} and district officials during their peak. The shrine buildings were burned down and later rebuilt at their current location. In {{ill|Tenshō|ja|天正}} 3 (1575), {{ill|Uesugi Kenshin|ja|上杉謙信}} offered a prayer document to the shrine, praying for victory against {{ill|Hōjō Ujizane|ja|北条氏政}}{{ill|Uesugi Kenshin prayer document|ja|上杉謙信願文集}}. In {{ill|Kanei|ja|寛永}} 1 (1624), the Tokugawa shogunate granted 200 koku of shrine land to the shrine. In Meiji 1 (1868), following the separation of Shinto and Buddhism ({{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|ja|神仏分離}}), the shrine was renamed "Takemizuwake Shrine" from "Hachiman Shrine," reflecting the disbanding of the associated temple ({{ill|Shinano Five Mountains|ja|信濃五山}}). The shrine was initially classified as a village shrine ({{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}) in the Modern Shrine ranking System but was promoted to a prefectural shrine ({{ill|Kensha|ja|県社}}) in Meiji 41 (1908). In 1876, the traditional Buddhist ceremony, the Grand Head festival ({{ill|Daitōsai|ja|大頭祭}}), was transformed into a Shinto ritual吉永みち子『もっと馬を!』平凡社、1990年、8 - 20ページ「木曽馬の村」. === Shrine ranks === * Jogan 8 (866) June, promoted from no rank to Junior Second rank (『{{ill|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|ja|日本三代実録}}』) * Jogan 9 (867) March 26, listed as a government shrine (『日本三代実録』) == Shrine Grounds == [[File:Takemizuwake-jinja honden.JPG|thumb|210px|right|{{center|Honden}}]] [[File:Takemizuwake-jinja keidai.JPG|thumb|210px|right|{{center|Shrine Grove (Nagano Prefecture designated natural monument)}}]] The shrine grounds cover 18,896 square meters and include a grove primarily composed of zelkova and cedar trees, with over 20 species and 400 trees in total. Many of the trees are old, and the "Takemizuwake Shrine Grove" is designated as a natural monument by Nagano Prefecture. The grounds, measuring approximately 280 meters from north to south and 70 meters from east to west, were originally square but were eroded into their current rectangular shape by frequent floods from the Chikuma River. A document from the Kanei era (1624-1644) was recently discovered, showing a square layout. Most of the current shrine buildings were constructed after a fire in Tenpō 13 (1842). The main hall was completed in Kaei 3 (1850) by Tatekawa Washiro II from Suwa. The worship hall was completed in Ansei 3 (1856) by Mineura Yagorō under Tatekawa Washiro's supervision. The main hall of the subsidiary Kōra Shrine is the oldest building, having survived the fire. The associated temple, known as Sarashina Hachiman Jinguji, was one of the Shinano Five Mountains of the Tendai sect but was abolished during the Meiji period's anti-Buddhist movement ({{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|ja|廃仏毀釈}}). == Subsidiary Shrines == === Subsidiary Shrines === [[File:Takemizuwake-jinja Kora-sha.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{center|Kōra Shrine}}{{small|The main hall inside the covering structure is a Nagano Prefecture treasure.}}]] * Kōra Shrine (高良社) *: The main hall inside the covering structure is the oldest in the shrine grounds, believed to have been built in the late Muromachi period (16th century). It is designated as a Nagano Prefecture treasureExplanatory panel on-site.. === Associated Shrines === * Emperor Jimmu Shrine * Smallpox Shrine * Sake Brewer Shrine * Yaegaki Shrine * Sukune Shrine * Komagata Shrine * Kojin Shrine * Twelve Shrines * Tenjin Shrine * Koyasu Shrine * Ten stone shrines: Ontake Shrine, Kotohira Shrine, Tōshōgū, Myōgi Shrine, Seki no Kami, Dōsojin, Water God Shrine, Mountain God Shrine, Akiba Shrine, Kashima Shrine == festivals == === annual festivals === The festivals held at Takemizuwake Shrine are as follows. Particularly notable are the three major festivals: the Prayer festival (March 15), the Grand festival (September 15), and the Grand Head festival (New Harvest festival, December 10-14).
annual festivals List
The three major festivals are in boldfestivals according to the shrine history.. * Monthly ** Monthly festival (1st, 5th, 28th) ** Usagi Day festival (Usagi Day) * January ** New Year's festival (January 1) ** Rice Planting festival (January 5) ** New Year's festival (January 15) * February ** Setsubun festival (Setsubun Day in February) ** National Foundation Day festival (February 11) * March ** '''Prayer festival''' (March 15) ** First Usagi Lecture festival (Old Calendar February Usagi Day) * April ** Higime Lecture Society festival (Mid-April) ** Spring festival (April 28) * June ** Great Purification ceremony (June 30) * July ** Kashiwa festival (July 15) * September ** Yaejime festival (September 1) ** Mid-Autumn festival (September 14) ** '''Grand festival''' (September 15) ** Autumn festival (September 24) * November ** Meiji Day festival (November 3) * December ** Kama Purification Ritual (December 3) ** '''Grand Head festival (New Harvest festival)''' (December 10-14) ** Emperor's Birthday festival (December 23) ** Great Purification ceremony, New Year's Eve festival (December 31)
=== Grand Head festival === The Grand Head festival (Niinamesai) held from December 10 to 14 is called the "Daitōsai". The festival is led by five headmen, with the third headman being called "Daitō," giving the festival its name. The "Headman's Record" (御頭帳) traces back to Bunroku 1 (1592), making it a festival with a history of over 400 years. It is designated as an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan. == Cultural Properties == === Selected Intangible Folk Cultural Property (National Selection) === * Headman's ceremony of Takemizuwake Shrine - Selected on December 17, 1986{{Cultural Property Database|312|353|Headman's ceremony of Takemizuwake Shrine}}. === Nagano Prefecture Designated Cultural Properties === * Nagano Prefecture Treasures (Tangible Cultural Properties) ** main hall of Kōra Shrine (Building) - Muromachi period. Designated on July 21, 1975. ** Bronze Hanging Lantern (Craft) - Muromachi period. Designated on April 13, 1970. * Natural Monument ** Takemizuwake Shrine Grove - Designated on February 25, 1965. * Historic Site ** Takemizuwake Shrine Matsuda House Site - Medieval period. {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Takemizuwake Shrine | image = Takemizuwake-jinja shaden.JPG |caption = From right: Chokushiden, Haiden, Honden | location = {{ill|Chikuma, Nagano|ja|千曲市}}, Nagano Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{coord|36|31|10.08|N|138|06|10.71|E|region:JP-20_type:landmark|display=inline,title|name=Takemizuwake Shrine}} | deity = {{ill|Takemizuwake no Ōkami|ja|武美名別命}} | object = | rank = {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} ({{ill|Myojin Taisha|ja|名神大}})
Fourth shrine of {{ill|Shinano Province|ja|信濃国}}
Former {{ill|Prefectural shrine|ja|県社}}
{{ill|Beppyo Shrine|ja|別表神社}} | established = During the reign of the 8th Emperor {{ill|Emperor Kōgen|ja|孝元天皇}} (trad.) | architecture = Nagare-zukuri | nickname = Hachiman Shrine | pilgrimage = | festival = September 15 | rituals = Daitōsai (Niinamesai), December 10-14 | map = Japan Nagano Prefecture | label = Takemizuwake Shrine | relief = 1 | map_width = 256 }} [[File:Takemizuwake-jinja ootorii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{center|Ōtorii}}]] '''Takemizuwake Shrine''' (武水別神社[[ja:武水別神社]]) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Chikuma, Nagano|ja|千曲市}}, Nagano Prefecture, Japan. It is a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} ({{ill|Myojin Taisha|ja|名神大}}) and the fourth shrine of {{ill|Shinano Province|ja|信濃国}}. It was formerly classified as a {{ill|Prefectural shrine|ja|県社}} and is now a {{ill|Beppyo Shrine|ja|別表神社}} under the Association of Shinto Shrines. The shrine's old name was "Hachiman Shrine," and it is still commonly referred to as "Yawata-sama" or "Yawata Shrine." == deity == '''Main deity''' * '''{{ill|Takemizuwake no Ōkami|ja|武美名別命}}''' (Takemizuwake no Ōkami)According to the shrine's history. *: The shrine's tradition states that this deity was enshrined to pray for the fertility of the Zenkoji Plain and to prevent the flooding of the Chikuma River. '''Deities in the Same Shrine''' : The three deities enshrined together here collectively represent the {{ill|Hachiman deity|ja|八幡神}}. * Hondawake no Mikoto (誉田別命, {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|ja|応神天皇}}) * Okinagatarashihime no Mikoto (息長足比売命, {{ill|Empress Jingū|ja|神功皇后}}) * Hime Ōkami (比咩大神) == History == === Overview === According to shrine tradition, it was established during the reign of the 8th Emperor {{ill|Emperor Kōgen|ja|孝元天皇}}Shrine history.. The earliest record in historical documents is from {{ill|Jogan|ja|貞観}} 8 (866), when it was given the rank of {{ill|Junior Second rank|ja|従二位}} from no rank. Additionally, it is listed as "Takemizuwake Shrine" in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}} compiled in {{ill|Engi|ja|延長}} 5 (927), categorized as a {{ill|Myojin Taisha|ja|名神大}}. However, the evidence supporting the identification of this shrine as the one mentioned in the documents is not definitive『日本の神々』 Takemizuwake Shrine entry., and another candidate is {{ill|Okeno Omi Shrine|ja|桶知大神社}} in Nagano City. The area around Takemizuwake Shrine became an estate ({{ill|Shōen|ja|荘園}}) of {{ill|Iwashimizu Hachiman Shrine|ja|石清水八幡宮}} (Otani estate) from the late Heian period, and it is said that the Hachiman deity (the three deities enshrined together) was invited from Iwashimizu Hachiman Shrine during the Anwa era (968-970). The Hachiman deity is known as the tutelary deity of the {{ill|Minamoto clan|ja|源氏}}, and Takemizuwake Shrine was widely revered by warriors as the foremost Hachiman Shrine in the region. It is also said that {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshinaka|ja|源義仲}} prayed here『参考源平盛衰記』 mentions on June 25 (or 14), Yōwa 1 (1181), that "八幡社ヲ伏拝ミ". However, it is unclear if this "Hachiman Shrine" is the same as Takemizuwake Shrine.. In {{ill|Hōgen|ja|保元}} 3 (1158), there is a record of lands in Otani estate, Sarashina District being confiscated by multiple officials. On that day, a government order was issued to halt thisIwashimizu document. During the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}} (1335), the Four Shrine clan, who served as Shinto priests of Takemizuwake Shrine, together with the Hoshina and Sekiya clans, attacked the {{ill|Shugo|ja|守護所}} (provincial headquarters) in Funeiyama (Suwa), but were suppressed. This resulted in the downfall of the Four Shrine clan, who were said to have served as both {{ill|Jitō|ja|地頭}} and district officials during their peak. The shrine buildings were burned down and later rebuilt at their current location. In {{ill|Tenshō|ja|天正}} 3 (1575), {{ill|Uesugi Kenshin|ja|上杉謙信}} offered a prayer document to the shrine, praying for victory against {{ill|Hōjō Ujizane|ja|北条氏政}}{{ill|Uesugi Kenshin prayer document|ja|上杉謙信願文集}}. In {{ill|Kanei|ja|寛永}} 1 (1624), the Tokugawa shogunate granted 200 koku of shrine land to the shrine. In Meiji 1 (1868), following the separation of Shinto and Buddhism ({{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|ja|神仏分離}}), the shrine was renamed "Takemizuwake Shrine" from "Hachiman Shrine," reflecting the disbanding of the associated temple ({{ill|Shinano Five Mountains|ja|信濃五山}}). The shrine was initially classified as a village shrine ({{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}) in the Modern Shrine ranking System but was promoted to a prefectural shrine ({{ill|Kensha|ja|県社}}) in Meiji 41 (1908). In 1876, the traditional Buddhist ceremony, the Grand Head festival ({{ill|Daitōsai|ja|大頭祭}}), was transformed into a Shinto ritual吉永みち子『もっと馬を!』平凡社、1990年、8 - 20ページ「木曽馬の村」. === Shrine ranks === * Jogan 8 (866) June, promoted from no rank to Junior Second rank (『{{ill|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|ja|日本三代実録}}』) * Jogan 9 (867) March 26, listed as a government shrine (『日本三代実録』) == Shrine Grounds == [[File:Takemizuwake-jinja honden.JPG|thumb|210px|right|{{center|Honden}}]] [[File:Takemizuwake-jinja keidai.JPG|thumb|210px|right|{{center|Shrine Grove (Nagano Prefecture designated natural monument)}}]] The shrine grounds cover 18,896 square meters and include a grove primarily composed of zelkova and cedar trees, with over 20 species and 400 trees in total. Many of the trees are old, and the "Takemizuwake Shrine Grove" is designated as a natural monument by Nagano Prefecture. The grounds, measuring approximately 280 meters from north to south and 70 meters from east to west, were originally square but were eroded into their current rectangular shape by frequent floods from the Chikuma River. A document from the Kanei era (1624-1644) was recently discovered, showing a square layout. Most of the current shrine buildings were constructed after a fire in Tenpō 13 (1842). The main hall was completed in Kaei 3 (1850) by Tatekawa Washiro II from Suwa. The worship hall was completed in Ansei 3 (1856) by Mineura Yagorō under Tatekawa Washiro's supervision. The main hall of the subsidiary Kōra Shrine is the oldest building, having survived the fire. The associated temple, known as Sarashina Hachiman Jinguji, was one of the Shinano Five Mountains of the Tendai sect but was abolished during the Meiji period's anti-Buddhist movement ({{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|ja|廃仏毀釈}}). == Subsidiary Shrines == === Subsidiary Shrines === [[File:Takemizuwake-jinja Kora-sha.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{center|Kōra Shrine}}{{small|The main hall inside the covering structure is a Nagano Prefecture treasure.}}]] * Kōra Shrine (高良社) *: The main hall inside the covering structure is the oldest in the shrine grounds, believed to have been built in the late Muromachi period (16th century). It is designated as a Nagano Prefecture treasureExplanatory panel on-site.. === Associated Shrines === * Emperor Jimmu Shrine * Smallpox Shrine * Sake Brewer Shrine * Yaegaki Shrine * Sukune Shrine * Komagata Shrine * Kojin Shrine * Twelve Shrines * Tenjin Shrine * Koyasu Shrine * Ten stone shrines: Ontake Shrine, Kotohira Shrine, Tōshōgū, Myōgi Shrine, Seki no Kami, Dōsojin, Water God Shrine, Mountain God Shrine, Akiba Shrine, Kashima Shrine == festivals == === annual festivals === The festivals held at Takemizuwake Shrine are as follows. Particularly notable are the three major festivals: the Prayer festival (March 15), the Grand festival (September 15), and the Grand Head festival (New Harvest festival, December 10-14).

The area around Takemizuwake Shrine became an estate ({{ill|Shōen|ja|荘園}}) of {{ill|Iwashimizu Hachiman Shrine|ja|石清水八幡宮}} (Otani estate) from the late Heian period, and it is said that the Hachiman deity (the three deities enshrined together) was invited from Iwashimizu Hachiman Shrine during the Anwa era (968-970). The Hachiman deity is known as the tutelary deity of the {{ill|Minamoto clan|ja|源氏}}, and Takemizuwake Shrine was widely revered by warriors as the foremost Hachiman Shrine in the region. It is also said that {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshinaka|ja|源義仲}} prayed here『参考源平盛衰記』 mentions on June 25 (or 14), Yōwa 1 (1181), that "八幡社ヲ伏拝ミ". However, it is unclear if this "Hachiman Shrine" is the same as Takemizuwake Shrine.. In {{ill|Hōgen|ja|保元}} 3 (1158), there is a record of lands in Otani estate, Sarashina District being confiscated by multiple officials. This resulted in the downfall of the Four Shrine clan, who were said to have served as both {{ill|Jitō|ja|地頭}} and district officials during their peak. However, the evidence supporting the identification of this shrine as the one mentioned in the documents is not definitive『日本の神々』 Takemizuwake Shrine entry., and another candidate is {{ill|Okeno Omi Shrine|ja|桶知大神社}} in Nagano City. The area around Takemizuwake Shrine became an estate ({{ill|Shōen|ja|荘園}}) of {{ill|Iwashimizu Hachiman Shrine|ja|石清水八幡宮}} (Otani estate) from the late Heian period, and it is said that the Hachiman deity (the three deities enshrined together) was invited from Iwashimizu Hachiman Shrine during the Anwa era (968-970). The Hachiman deity is known as the tutelary deity of the {{ill|Minamoto clan|ja|源氏}}, and Takemizuwake Shrine was widely revered by warriors as the foremost Hachiman Shrine in the region. It is also said that {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshinaka|ja|源義仲}} prayed here『参考源平盛衰記』 mentions on June 25 (or 14), Yōwa 1 (1181), that "八幡社ヲ伏拝ミ". However, it is unclear if this "Hachiman Shrine" is the same as Takemizuwake Shrine.. In {{ill|Hōgen|ja|保元}} 3 (1158), there is a record of lands in Otani estate, Sarashina District being confiscated by multiple officials. On that day, a government order was issued to halt thisIwashimizu document. During the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}} (1335), the Four Shrine clan, who served as Shinto priests of Takemizuwake Shrine, together with the Hoshina and Sekiya clans, attacked the {{ill|Shugo|ja|守護所}} (provincial headquarters) in Funeiyama (Suwa), but were suppressed. This resulted in the downfall of the Four Shrine clan, who were said to have served as both {{ill|Jitō|ja|地頭}} and district officials during their peak. The shrine buildings were burned down and later rebuilt at their current location. In {{ill|Tenshō|ja|天正}} 3 (1575), {{ill|Uesugi Kenshin|ja|上杉謙信}} offered a prayer document to the shrine, praying for victory against {{ill|Hōjō Ujizane|ja|北条氏政}}{{ill|Uesugi Kenshin prayer document|ja|上杉謙信願文集}}. In {{ill|Kanei|ja|寛永}} 1 (1624), the Tokugawa shogunate granted 200 koku of shrine land to the shrine. In Meiji 1 (1868), following the separation of Shinto and Buddhism ({{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|ja|神仏分離}}), the shrine was renamed "Takemizuwake Shrine" from "Hachiman Shrine," reflecting the disbanding of the associated temple ({{ill|Shinano Five Mountains|ja|信濃五山}}). The shrine was initially classified as a village shrine ({{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}) in the Modern Shrine ranking System but was promoted to a prefectural shrine ({{ill|Kensha|ja|県社}}) in Meiji 41 (1908). In 1876, the traditional Buddhist ceremony, the Grand Head festival ({{ill|Daitōsai|ja|大頭祭}}), was transformed into a Shinto ritual吉永みち子『もっと馬を!』平凡社、1990年、8 - 20ページ「木曽馬の村」. === Shrine ranks === * Jogan 8 (866) June, promoted from no rank to Junior Second rank (『{{ill|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|ja|日本三代実録}}』) * Jogan 9 (867) March 26, listed as a government shrine (『日本三代実録』) == Shrine Grounds == [[File:Takemizuwake-jinja honden.JPG|thumb|210px|right|{{center|Honden}}]] [[File:Takemizuwake-jinja keidai.JPG|thumb|210px|right|{{center|Shrine Grove (Nagano Prefecture designated natural monument)}}]] The shrine grounds cover 18,896 square meters and include a grove primarily composed of zelkova and cedar trees, with over 20 species and 400 trees in total. Many of the trees are old, and the "Takemizuwake Shrine Grove" is designated as a natural monument by Nagano Prefecture. The grounds, measuring approximately 280 meters from north to south and 70 meters from east to west, were originally square but were eroded into their current rectangular shape by frequent floods from the Chikuma River. A document from the Kanei era (1624-1644) was recently discovered, showing a square layout. Most of the current shrine buildings were constructed after a fire in Tenpō 13 (1842). The main hall was completed in Kaei 3 (1850) by Tatekawa Washiro II from Suwa. The worship hall was completed in Ansei 3 (1856) by Mineura Yagorō under Tatekawa Washiro's supervision. The main hall of the subsidiary Kōra Shrine is the oldest building, having survived the fire. The associated temple, known as Sarashina Hachiman Jinguji, was one of the Shinano Five Mountains of the Tendai sect but was abolished during the Meiji period's anti-Buddhist movement ({{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|ja|廃仏毀釈}}). == Subsidiary Shrines == === Subsidiary Shrines === [[File:Takemizuwake-jinja Kora-sha.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{center|Kōra Shrine}}{{small|The main hall inside the covering structure is a Nagano Prefecture treasure.}}]] * Kōra Shrine (高良社) *: The main hall inside the covering structure is the oldest in the shrine grounds, believed to have been built in the late Muromachi period (16th century). It is designated as a Nagano Prefecture treasureExplanatory panel on-site.. === Associated Shrines === * Emperor Jimmu Shrine * Smallpox Shrine * Sake Brewer Shrine * Yaegaki Shrine * Sukune Shrine * Komagata Shrine * Kojin Shrine * Twelve Shrines * Tenjin Shrine * Koyasu Shrine * Ten stone shrines: Ontake Shrine, Kotohira Shrine, Tōshōgū, Myōgi Shrine, Seki no Kami, Dōsojin, Water God Shrine, Mountain God Shrine, Akiba Shrine, Kashima Shrine == festivals == === festivals === The festivals held at Takemizuwake Shrine are as follows. Particularly notable are the three major festivals: the Prayer festival (March 15), the Grand festival (September 15), and the Grand Head festival (New Harvest festival, December 10-14).

=== Grand Head festival === The Grand Head festival (Niinamesai) held from December 10 to 14 is called the "Daitōsai". The festival is led by five headmen, with the third headman being called "Daitō," giving the festival its name. The "Headman's Record" (御頭帳) traces back to Bunroku 1 (1592), making it a festival with a history of over 400 years. {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Takemizuwake Shrine | image = Takemizuwake-jinja shaden.JPG |caption = From right: Chokushiden, Haiden, Honden | location = {{ill|Chikuma, Nagano|ja|千曲市}}, Nagano Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{coord|36|31|10.08|N|138|06|10.71|E|region:JP-20_type:landmark|display=inline,title|name=Takemizuwake Shrine}} | deity = {{ill|Takemizuwake no Ōkami|ja|武美名別命}} | object = | type = {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} ({{ill|Myojin Taisha|ja|名神大}})
Fourth shrine of {{ill|Shinano Province|ja|信濃国}}
Former {{ill|Prefectural shrine|ja|県社}}
{{ill|Beppyo Shrine|ja|別表神社}} | established = During the reign of the 8th Emperor {{ill|Emperor Kōgen|ja|孝元天皇}} (trad.) | architecture = Nagare-zukuri | nickname = Hachiman Shrine | pilgrimage = | festival = September 15 | rituals = Daitōsai (Niinamesai), December 10-14 | map = Japan Nagano Prefecture | label = Takemizuwake Shrine | relief = 1 | map_width = 256 }} [[File:Takemizuwake-jinja ootorii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{center|Ōtorii}}]] '''Takemizuwake Shrine''' (武水別神社[[ja:武水別神社]]) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Chikuma, Nagano|ja|千曲市}}, Nagano Prefecture, Japan. It is a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} ({{ill|Myojin Taisha|ja|名神大}}) and the fourth shrine of {{ill|Shinano Province|ja|信濃国}}. It was formerly classified as a {{ill|Prefectural shrine|ja|県社}} and is now a {{ill|Beppyo Shrine|ja|別表神社}} under the Association of Shinto Shrines. The shrine's old name was "Hachiman Shrine," and it is still commonly referred to as "Yawata-sama" or "Yawata Shrine." == deity == '''Main deity''' * '''{{ill|Takemizuwake no Ōkami|ja|武美名別命}}''' (Takemizuwake no Ōkami)According to the shrine's history. *: The shrine's tradition states that this deity was enshrined to pray for the fertility of the Zenkoji Plain and to prevent the flooding of the Chikuma River. '''Deities in the Same Shrine''' : The three deities enshrined together here collectively represent the {{ill|Hachiman deity|ja|八幡神}}. * Hondawake no Mikoto (誉田別命, {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|ja|応神天皇}}) * Okinagatarashihime no Mikoto (息長足比売命, {{ill|Empress Jingū|ja|神功皇后}}) * Hime Ōkami (比咩大神) == History == === Overview === According to shrine tradition, it was established during the reign of the 8th Emperor {{ill|Emperor Kōgen|ja|孝元天皇}}Shrine history.. The earliest record in historical documents is from {{ill|Jogan|ja|貞観}} 8 (866), when it was given the rank of {{ill|Junior Second rank|ja|従二位}} from no rank. Additionally, it is listed as "Takemizuwake Shrine" in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}} compiled in {{ill|Engi|ja|延長}} 5 (927), categorized as a {{ill|Myojin Taisha|ja|名神大}}. However, the evidence supporting the identification of this shrine as the one mentioned in the documents is not definitive『日本の神々』 Takemizuwake Shrine entry., and another candidate is {{ill|Okeno Omi Shrine|ja|桶知大神社}} in Nagano City. The area around Takemizuwake Shrine became an estate ({{ill|Shōen|ja|荘園}}) of {{ill|Iwashimizu Hachiman Shrine|ja|石清水八幡宮}} (Otani estate) from the late Heian period, and it is said that the Hachiman deity (the three deities enshrined together) was invited from Iwashimizu Hachiman Shrine during the Anwa era (968-970). The Hachiman deity is known as the tutelary deity of the {{ill|Minamoto clan|ja|源氏}}, and Takemizuwake Shrine was widely revered by warriors as the foremost Hachiman Shrine in the region. It is also said that {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshinaka|ja|源義仲}} prayed here『参考源平盛衰記』 mentions on June 25 (or 14), Yōwa 1 (1181), that "八幡社ヲ伏拝ミ". However, it is unclear if this "Hachiman Shrine" is the same as Takemizuwake Shrine.. In {{ill|Hōgen|ja|保元}} 3 (1158), there is a record of lands in Otani estate, Sarashina District being confiscated by multiple officials. On that day, a government order was issued to halt thisIwashimizu document. During the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}} (1335), the Four Shrine clan, who served as Shinto priests of Takemizuwake Shrine, together with the Hoshina and Sekiya clans, attacked the {{ill|Shugo|ja|守護所}} (provincial headquarters) in Funeiyama (Suwa), but were suppressed. This resulted in the downfall of the Four Shrine clan, who were said to have served as both {{ill|Jitō|ja|地頭}} and district officials during their peak. The shrine buildings were burned down and later rebuilt at their current location. In {{ill|Tenshō|ja|天正}} 3 (1575), {{ill|Uesugi Kenshin|ja|上杉謙信}} offered a prayer document to the shrine, praying for victory against {{ill|Hōjō Ujizane|ja|北条氏政}}{{ill|Uesugi Kenshin prayer document|ja|上杉謙信願文集}}. In {{ill|Kanei|ja|寛永}} 1 (1624), the Tokugawa shogunate granted 200 koku of shrine land to the shrine. In Meiji 1 (1868), following the separation of Shinto and Buddhism ({{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|ja|神仏分離}}), the shrine was renamed "Takemizuwake Shrine" from "Hachiman Shrine," reflecting the disbanding of the associated temple ({{ill|Shinano Five Mountains|ja|信濃五山}}). The shrine was initially classified as a village shrine ({{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}) in the Modern Shrine ranking System but was promoted to a prefectural shrine ({{ill|Kensha|ja|県社}}) in Meiji 41 (1908). In 1876, the traditional Buddhist ceremony, the Grand Head festival ({{ill|Daitōsai|ja|大頭祭}}), was transformed into a Shinto ritual吉永みち子『もっと馬を!』平凡社、1990年、8 - 20ページ「木曽馬の村」. === Shrine ranks === * Jogan 8 (866) June, promoted from no rank to Junior Second rank (『{{ill|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|ja|日本三代実録}}』) * Jogan 9 (867) March 26, listed as a government shrine (『日本三代実録』) == Shrine Grounds == [[File:Takemizuwake-jinja honden.JPG|thumb|210px|right|{{center|Honden}}]] [[File:Takemizuwake-jinja keidai.JPG|thumb|210px|right|{{center|Shrine Grove (Nagano Prefecture designated natural monument)}}]] The shrine grounds cover 18,896 square meters and include a grove primarily composed of zelkova and cedar trees, with over 20 species and 400 trees in total. Many of the trees are old, and the "Takemizuwake Shrine Grove" is designated as a natural monument by Nagano Prefecture. The grounds, measuring approximately 280 meters from north to south and 70 meters from east to west, were originally square but were eroded into their current rectangular shape by frequent floods from the Chikuma River. A document from the Kanei era (1624-1644) was recently discovered, showing a square layout. Most of the current shrine buildings were constructed after a fire in Tenpō 13 (1842). The main hall was completed in Kaei 3 (1850) by Tatekawa Washiro II from Suwa. The worship hall was completed in Ansei 3 (1856) by Mineura Yagorō under Tatekawa Washiro's supervision. The main hall of the subsidiary Kōra Shrine is the oldest building, having survived the fire. The associated temple, known as Sarashina Hachiman Jinguji, was one of the Shinano Five Mountains of the Tendai sect but was abolished during the Meiji period's anti-Buddhist movement ({{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|ja|廃仏毀釈}}). == Subsidiary Shrines == === Subsidiary Shrines === [[File:Takemizuwake-jinja Kora-sha.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{center|Kōra Shrine}}{{small|The main hall inside the covering structure is a Nagano Prefecture treasure.}}]] * Kōra Shrine (高良社) *: The main hall inside the covering structure is the oldest in the shrine grounds, believed to have been built in the late Muromachi period (16th century). It is designated as a Nagano Prefecture treasureExplanatory panel on-site.. === Associated Shrines === * Emperor Jimmu Shrine * Smallpox Shrine * Sake Brewer Shrine * Yaegaki Shrine * Sukune Shrine * Komagata Shrine * Kojin Shrine * Twelve Shrines * Tenjin Shrine * Koyasu Shrine * Ten stone shrines: Ontake Shrine, Kotohira Shrine, Tōshōgū, Myōgi Shrine, Seki no Kami, Dōsojin, Water God Shrine, Mountain God Shrine, Akiba Shrine, Kashima Shrine == festivals == === festivals === The festivals held at Takemizuwake Shrine are as follows. Particularly notable are the three major festivals: the Prayer festival (March 15), the Grand festival (September 15), and the Grand Head festival (New Harvest festival, December 10-14).
festivals List
The three major festivals are in boldfestivals according to the shrine history.. * Monthly ** Monthly festival (1st, 5th, 28th) ** Usagi Day festival (Usagi Day) * January ** New Year's festival (January 1) ** Rice Planting festival (January 5) ** New Year's festival (January 15) * February ** Setsubun festival (Setsubun Day in February) ** National Foundation Day festival (February 11) * March ** '''Prayer festival''' (March 15) ** First Usagi Lecture festival (Old Calendar February Usagi Day) * April ** Higime Lecture Society festival (Mid-April) ** Spring festival (April 28) * June ** Great Purification ceremony (June 30) * July ** Kashiwa festival (July 15) * September ** Yaejime festival (September 1) ** Mid-Autumn festival (September 14) ** '''Grand festival''' (September 15) ** Autumn festival (September 24) * November ** Meiji Day festival (November 3) * December ** Kama Purification Ritual (December 3) ** '''Grand Head festival (New Harvest festival)''' (December 10-14) ** Emperor's Birthday festival (December 23) ** Great Purification ceremony, New Year's Eve festival (December 31)
=== Grand Head festival === The Grand Head festival (Niinamesai) held from December 10 to 14 is called the "Daitōsai". The festival is led by five headmen, with the third headman being called "Daitō," giving the festival its name. The "Headman's Record" (御頭帳) traces back to Bunroku 1 (1592), making it a festival with a history of over 400 years. It is designated as an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan. == Cultural Properties == === Selected Intangible Folk Cultural Property (National Selection) === * Headman's ceremony of Takemizuwake Shrine - Selected on December 17, 1986{{Cultural Property Database|312|353|Headman's ceremony of Takemizuwake Shrine}}. === Nagano Prefecture Designated Cultural Properties === * Nagano Prefecture Treasures (Tangible Cultural Properties) ** main hall of Kōra Shrine (Building) - Muromachi period. Designated on July 21, 1975. ** Bronze Hanging Lantern (Craft) - Muromachi period. Designated on April 13, 1970. * Natural Monument ** Takemizuwake Shrine Grove - Designated on February 25, 1965. * Historic Site ** Takemizuwake Shrine Matsuda House Site - Medieval period. Designated on April 20, 2006. == Visitor Information == '''location''' * Yawata 3012, Chikuma City, Nagano Prefecture, Japan '''Nearby''' * {{ill|Inariyama-juku|ja|稲荷山宿}} - A {{ill|Post station|ja|宿場}} on the {{ill|Zenkoji Kaido|ja|善光寺街道}} ({{ill|Hokkokukaidō|ja|北国西街道}}, Zenkoji Nishi Kaido). * {{ill|Mount Obasute|ja|姨捨山}} == Notes == {{reflist|group="note"}} == References == {{reflist}} == Further Reading == * Shrine history * {{Cite book|Japanese|editor=|author=|year=1979|chapter=Takemizuwake Shrine|title={{ill|Nihon Rekishi Chimei Taikei|ja|日本歴史地名大系}} 20 Nagano Prefecture|publisher={{ill|Heibonsha|ja|平凡社}}|isbn=4582490204|ref={{Harvid|Takemizuwake Shrine (Heibonsha)|1979}}}} * Hayashi Yukiyoshi, "Takemizuwake Shrine" in {{ill|Japanese Gods - Shrines and Holy Places - 9 Mino, Hida, Shinano|ja|谷川健一 編『日本の神々 -神社と聖地- 9 美濃・飛騨・信濃'}} (2000, {{ill|Hakusuisha|ja|白水社}}) == Related Articles == {{Commonscat|Takemizuwake Shrine}} * {{ill|Okeno Omi Shrine|ja|桶知大神社}} (Nagano City) - Another candidate for the {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} "Takemizuwake Shrine." * {{ill|Motohachiman|ja|本八幡}} - The site where the deity from Iwashimizu Hachiman Shrine was enshrined in 968. * {{ill|namerii Stone|ja|男女離石}} - {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Takemizuwake Shrine | image = Takemizuwake-jinja shaden.JPG |caption = From right: Chokushiden, Haiden, Honden | location = {{ill|Chikuma, Nagano|ja|千曲市}}, Nagano Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{coord|36|31|10.08|N|138|06|10.71|E|region:JP-20_type:landmark|display=inline,title|name=Takemizuwake Shrine}} | deity = {{ill|Takemizuwake no Ōkami|ja|武美名別命}} | object = | type = {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} ({{ill|Myojin Taisha|ja|名神大}})
Fourth shrine of {{ill|Shinano Province|ja|信濃国}}
Former {{ill|Prefectural shrine|ja|県社}}
{{ill|Beppyo Shrine|ja|別表神社}} | established = During the reign of the 8th Emperor {{ill|Emperor Kōgen|ja|孝元天皇}} (trad.) | architecture = Nagare-zukuri | nickname = Hachiman Shrine | pilgrimage = | festival = September 15 | rituals = Daitōsai (Niinamesai), December 10-14 | map = Japan Nagano Prefecture | label = Takemizuwake Shrine | relief = 1 | map_width = 256 }} [[File:Takemizuwake-jinja ootorii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{center|Ōtorii}}]] '''Takemizuwake Shrine''' (武水別神社[[ja:武水別神社]]) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Chikuma, Nagano|ja|千曲市}}, Nagano Prefecture, Japan. It is a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} ({{ill|Myojin Taisha|ja|名神大}}) and the fourth shrine of {{ill|Shinano Province|ja|信濃国}}. It was formerly classified as a {{ill|Prefectural shrine|ja|県社}} and is now a {{ill|Beppyo Shrine|ja|別表神社}} under the Association of Shinto Shrines. The shrine's old name was "Hachiman Shrine," and it is still commonly referred to as "Yawata-sama" or "Yawata Shrine." == deity == '''Main deity''' * '''{{ill|Takemizuwake no Ōkami|ja|武美名別命}}''' (Takemizuwake no Ōkami)According to the shrine's history. *: The shrine's tradition states that this deity was enshrined to pray for the fertility of the Zenkoji Plain and to prevent the flooding of the Chikuma River. '''Deities in the Same Shrine''' : The three deities enshrined together here collectively represent the {{ill|Hachiman deity|ja|八幡神}}. * Hondawake no Mikoto (誉田別命, {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|ja|応神天皇}}) * Okinagatarashihime no Mikoto (息長足比売命, {{ill|Empress Jingū|ja|神功皇后}}) * Hime Ōkami (比咩大神) == History == === Overview === According to shrine tradition, it was established during the reign of the 8th Emperor {{ill|Emperor Kōgen|ja|孝元天皇}}Shrine history.. The earliest record in historical documents is from {{ill|Jogan|ja|貞観}} 8 (866), when it was given the rank of {{ill|Junior Second rank|ja|従二位}} from no rank. Additionally, it is listed as "Takemizuwake Shrine" in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}} compiled in {{ill|Engi|ja|延長}} 5 (927), categorized as a {{ill|Myojin Taisha|ja|名神大}}. However, the evidence supporting the identification of this shrine as the one mentioned in the documents is not definitive『日本の神々』 Takemizuwake Shrine entry., and another candidate is {{ill|Okeno Omi Shrine|ja|桶知大神社}} in Nagano City. The area around Takemizuwake Shrine became an estate ({{ill|Shōen|ja|荘園}}) of {{ill|Iwashimizu Hachiman Shrine|ja|石清水八幡宮}} (Otani estate) from the late Heian period, and it is said that the Hachiman deity (the three deities enshrined together) was invited from Iwashimizu Hachiman Shrine during the Anwa era (968-970). The Hachiman deity is known as the tutelary deity of the {{ill|Minamoto clan|ja|源氏}}, and Takemizuwake Shrine was widely revered by warriors as the foremost Hachiman Shrine in the region. It is also said that {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshinaka|ja|源義仲}} prayed here『参考源平盛衰記』 mentions on June 25 (or 14), Yōwa 1 (1181), that "八幡社ヲ伏拝ミ". However, it is unclear if this "Hachiman Shrine" is the same as Takemizuwake Shrine.. In {{ill|Hōgen|ja|保元}} 3 (1158), there is a record of lands in Otani estate, Sarashina District being confiscated by multiple officials. On that day, a government order was issued to halt thisIwashimizu document. During the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}} (1335), the Four Shrine clan, who served as Shinto priests of Takemizuwake Shrine, together with the Hoshina and Sekiya clans, attacked the {{ill|Shugo|ja|守護所}} (provincial headquarters) in Funeiyama (Suwa), but were suppressed. This resulted in the downfall of the Four Shrine clan, who were said to have served as both {{ill|Jitō|ja|地頭}} and district officials during their peak. The shrine buildings were burned down and later rebuilt at their current location. In {{ill|Tenshō|ja|天正}} 3 (1575), {{ill|Uesugi Kenshin|ja|上杉謙信}} offered a prayer document to the shrine, praying for victory against {{ill|Hōjō Ujizane|ja|北条氏政}}{{ill|Uesugi Kenshin prayer document|ja|上杉謙信願文集}}. In {{ill|Kanei|ja|寛永}} 1 (1624), the Tokugawa shogunate granted 200 koku of shrine land to the shrine. In Meiji 1 (1868), following the separation of Shinto and Buddhism ({{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|ja|神仏分離}}), the shrine was renamed "Takemizuwake Shrine" from "Hachiman Shrine," reflecting the disbanding of the associated temple ({{ill|Shinano Five Mountains|ja|信濃五山}}). The shrine was initially classified as a village shrine ({{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}) in the Modern Shrine ranking System but was promoted to a prefectural shrine ({{ill|Kensha|ja|県社}}) in Meiji 41 (1908). In 1876, the traditional Buddhist ceremony, the Grand Head festival ({{ill|Daitōsai|ja|大頭祭}}), was transformed into a Shinto ritual吉永みち子『もっと馬を!』平凡社、1990年、8 - 20ページ「木曽馬の村」. === Shrine ranks === * Jogan 8 (866) June, promoted from no rank to Junior Second rank (『{{ill|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|ja|日本三代実録}}』) * Jogan 9 (867) March 26, listed as a government shrine (『日本三代実録』) == Shrine Grounds == [[File:Takemizuwake-jinja honden.JPG|thumb|210px|right|{{center|Honden}}]] [[File:Takemizuwake-jinja keidai.JPG|thumb|210px|right|{{center|Shrine Grove (Nagano Prefecture designated natural monument)}}]] The shrine grounds cover 18,896 square meters and include a grove primarily composed of zelkova and cedar trees, with over 20 species and 400 trees in total. Many of the trees are old, and the "Takemizuwake Shrine Grove" is designated as a natural monument by Nagano Prefecture. The grounds, measuring approximately 280 meters from north to south and 70 meters from east to west, were originally square but were eroded into their current rectangular shape by frequent floods from the Chikuma River. A document from the Kanei era (1624-1644) was recently discovered, showing a square layout. Most of the current shrine buildings were constructed after a fire in Tenpō 13 (1842). The main hall was completed in Kaei 3 (1850) by Tatekawa Washiro II from Suwa. The worship hall was completed in Ansei 3 (1856) by Mineura Yagorō under Tatekawa Washiro's supervision. The main hall of the subsidiary Kōra Shrine is the oldest building, having survived the fire. The associated temple, known as Sarashina Hachiman Jinguji, was one of the Shinano Five Mountains of the Tendai sect but was abolished during the Meiji period's anti-Buddhist movement ({{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|ja|廃仏毀釈}}). == Subsidiary Shrines == === Subsidiary Shrines === [[File:Takemizuwake-jinja Kora-sha.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{center|Kōra Shrine}}{{small|The main hall inside the covering structure is a Nagano Prefecture treasure.}}]] * Kōra Shrine (高良社) *: The main hall inside the covering structure is the oldest in the shrine grounds, believed to have been built in the late Muromachi period (16th century). It is designated as a Nagano Prefecture treasureExplanatory panel on-site.. === Associated Shrines === * Emperor Jimmu Shrine * Smallpox Shrine * Sake Brewer Shrine * Yaegaki Shrine * Sukune Shrine * Komagata Shrine * Kojin Shrine * Twelve Shrines * Tenjin Shrine * Koyasu Shrine * Ten stone shrines: Ontake Shrine, Kotohira Shrine, Tōshōgū, Myōgi Shrine, Seki no Kami, Dōsojin, Water God Shrine, Mountain God Shrine, Akiba Shrine, Kashima Shrine == festivals == === festivals === The festivals held at Takemizuwake Shrine are as follows. Particularly notable are the three major festivals: the Prayer festival (March 15), the Grand festival (September 15), and the Grand Head festival (New Harvest festival, December 10-14).
festivals List
The three major festivals are in boldfestivals according to the shrine history.. * Monthly ** Monthly festival (1st, 5th, 28th) ** Usagi Day festival (Usagi Day) * January ** New Year's festival (January 1) ** Rice Planting festival (January 5) ** New Year's festival (January 15) * February ** Setsubun festival (Setsubun Day in February) ** National Foundation Day festival (February 11) * March ** '''Prayer festival''' (March 15) ** First Usagi Lecture festival (Old Calendar February Usagi Day) * April ** Higime Lecture Society festival (Mid-April) ** Spring festival (April 28) * June ** Great Purification ceremony (June 30) * July ** Kashiwa festival (July 15) * September ** Yaejime festival (September 1) ** Mid-Autumn festival (September 14) ** '''Grand festival''' (September 15) ** Autumn festival (September 24) * November ** Meiji Day festival (November 3) * December ** Kama Purification Ritual (December 3) ** '''Grand Head festival (New Harvest festival)''' (December 10-14) ** Emperor's Birthday festival (December 23) ** Great Purification ceremony, New Year's Eve festival (December 31)
=== Grand Head festival === The Grand Head festival (Niinamesai) held from December 10 to 14 is called the "Daitōsai". The festival is led by five headmen, with the third headman being called "Daitō," giving the festival its name. The "Headman's Record" (御頭帳) traces back to Bunroku 1 (1592), making it a festival with a history of over 400 years. Designated on July 21, 1975. ** Bronze Hanging Lantern (Craft) - Muromachi period. Designated on April 13, 1970. * Natural Monument ** Takemizuwake Shrine Grove - Designated on February 25, 1965. * Historic Site ** Takemizuwake Shrine Matsuda House Site - Medieval period. Designated on April 20, 2006. == Visitor Information == '''location''' * Yawata 3012, Chikuma City, Nagano Prefecture, Japan '''Nearby''' * {{ill|Inariyama-juku|ja|稲荷山宿}} - A {{ill|Post station|ja|宿場}} on the {{ill|Zenkoji Kaido|ja|善光寺街道}} ({{ill|Hokkokukaidō|ja|北国西街道}}, Zenkoji Nishi Kaido). * {{ill|Mount Obasute|ja|姨捨山}} == Notes == {{reflist|group="note"}} == References == {{reflist}} == Further Reading == * Shrine history * {{Cite book|Japanese|editor=|author=|year=1979|chapter=Takemizuwake Shrine|title={{ill|Nihon Rekishi Chimei Taikei|ja|日本歴史地名大系}} 20 Nagano Prefecture|publisher={{ill|Heibonsha|ja|平凡社}}|isbn=4582490204|ref={{Harvid|Takemizuwake Shrine (Heibonsha)|1979}}}} * Hayashi Yukiyoshi, "Takemizuwake Shrine" in {{ill|Japanese Gods - In 1876, the traditional Buddhist ceremony, the Grand Head festival ({{ill|Daitōsai|ja|大頭祭}}), was transformed into a Shinto ritual吉永みち子『もっと馬を!』平凡社、1990年、8 - 20ページ「木曽馬の村」. === Shrine ranks === * Jogan 8 (866) June, promoted from no rank to Junior Second rank (『{{ill|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|ja|日本三代実録}}』) * Jogan 9 (867) March 26, listed as a government shrine (『日本三代実録』) == Shrine Grounds == [[File:Takemizuwake-jinja honden.JPG|thumb|210px|right|{{center|Honden}}]] [[File:Takemizuwake-jinja keidai.JPG|thumb|210px|right|{{center|Shrine Grove (Nagano Prefecture designated natural monument)}}]] The shrine grounds cover 18,896 square meters and include a grove primarily composed of zelkova and cedar trees, with over 20 species and 400 trees in total. Many of the trees are old, and the "Takemizuwake Shrine Grove" is designated as a natural monument by Nagano Prefecture. The grounds, measuring approximately 280 meters from north to south and 70 meters from east to west, were originally square but were eroded into their current rectangular shape by frequent floods from the Chikuma River. A document from the Kanei era (1624-1644) was recently discovered, showing a square layout. Most of the current shrine buildings were constructed after a fire in Tenpō 13 (1842). The main hall was completed in Kaei 3 (1850) by Tatekawa Washiro II from Suwa. The worship hall was completed in Ansei 3 (1856) by Mineura Yagorō under Tatekawa Washiro's supervision. The main hall of the subsidiary Kōra Shrine is the oldest building, having survived the fire. The associated temple, known as Sarashina Hachiman Jinguji, was one of the Shinano Five Mountains of the Tendai sect but was abolished during the Meiji period's anti-Buddhist movement ({{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|ja|廃仏毀釈}}). == Subsidiary Shrines == === Subsidiary Shrines === [[File:Takemizuwake-jinja Kora-sha.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{center|Kōra Shrine}}{{small|The main hall inside the covering structure is a Nagano Prefecture treasure.}}]] * Kōra Shrine (高良社) *: The main hall inside the covering structure is the oldest in the shrine grounds, believed to have been built in the late Muromachi period (16th century). Particularly notable are the three major festivals: the Prayer festival (March 15), the Grand festival (September 15), and the Grand Head festival (New Harvest festival, December 10-14).

It is a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} ({{ill|Myojin Taisha|ja|名神大}}) and the fourth shrine of {{ill|Shinano Province|ja|信濃国}}. It was formerly classified as a {{ill|Prefectural shrine|ja|県社}} and is now a {{ill|Beppyo Shrine|ja|別表神社}} under the Association of Shinto Shrines. The shrine's old name was "Hachiman Shrine," and it is still commonly referred to as "Yawata-sama" or "Yawata Shrine." == deity == '''Main deity''' * '''{{ill|Takemizuwake no Ōkami|ja|武美名別命}}''' (Takemizuwake no Ōkami)According to the shrine's history. *: The shrine's tradition states that this deity was enshrined to pray for the fertility of the Zenkoji Plain and to prevent the flooding of the Chikuma River. '''Deities in the Same Shrine''' : The three deities enshrined together here collectively represent the {{ill|Hachiman deity|ja|八幡神}}. * Hondawake no Mikoto (誉田別命, {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|ja|応神天皇}}) * Okinagatarashihime no Mikoto (息長足比売命, {{ill|Empress Jingū|ja|神功皇后}}) * Hime Ōkami (比咩大神) == History == === Overview === According to shrine tradition, it was established during the reign of the 8th Emperor {{ill|Emperor Kōgen|ja|孝元天皇}}Shrine history.. The earliest record in historical documents is from {{ill|Jogan|ja|貞観}} 8 (866), when it was given the rank of {{ill|Junior Second rank|ja|従二位}} from no rank. Additionally, it is listed as "Takemizuwake Shrine" in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}} compiled in {{ill|Engi|ja|延長}} 5 (927), categorized as a {{ill|Myojin Taisha|ja|名神大}}. However, the evidence supporting the identification of this shrine as the one mentioned in the documents is not definitive『日本の神々』 Takemizuwake Shrine entry., and another candidate is {{ill|Okeno Omi Shrine|ja|桶知大神社}} in Nagano City. The area around Takemizuwake Shrine became an estate ({{ill|Shōen|ja|荘園}}) of {{ill|Iwashimizu Hachiman Shrine|ja|石清水八幡宮}} (Otani estate) from the late Heian period, and it is said that the Hachiman deity (the three deities enshrined together) was invited from Iwashimizu Hachiman Shrine during the Anwa era (968-970). The Hachiman deity is known as the tutelary deity of the {{ill|Minamoto clan|ja|源氏}}, and Takemizuwake Shrine was widely revered by warriors as the foremost Hachiman Shrine in the region. It is also said that {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshinaka|ja|源義仲}} prayed here『参考源平盛衰記』 mentions on June 25 (or 14), Yōwa 1 (1181), that "八幡社ヲ伏拝ミ". However, it is unclear if this "Hachiman Shrine" is the same as Takemizuwake Shrine.. In {{ill|Hōgen|ja|保元}} 3 (1158), there is a record of lands in Otani estate, Sarashina District being confiscated by multiple officials. On that day, a government order was issued to halt thisIwashimizu document. During the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}} (1335), the Four Shrine clan, who served as Shinto priests of Takemizuwake Shrine, together with the Hoshina and Sekiya clans, attacked the {{ill|Shugo|ja|守護所}} (provincial headquarters) in Funeiyama (Suwa), but were suppressed. This resulted in the downfall of the Four Shrine clan, who were said to have served as both {{ill|Jitō|ja|地頭}} and district officials during their peak. The shrine buildings were burned down and later rebuilt at their current location. In {{ill|Tenshō|ja|天正}} 3 (1575), {{ill|Uesugi Kenshin|ja|上杉謙信}} offered a prayer document to the shrine, praying for victory against {{ill|Hōjō Ujizane|ja|北条氏政}}{{ill|Uesugi Kenshin prayer document|ja|上杉謙信願文集}}. '''Deities in the Same Shrine''' : The three deities enshrined together here collectively represent the {{ill|Hachiman deity|ja|八幡神}}. * Hondawake no Mikoto (誉田別命, {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|ja|応神天皇}}) * Okinagatarashihime no Mikoto (息長足比売命, {{ill|Empress Jingū|ja|神功皇后}}) * Hime Ōkami (比咩大神) == History == === Overview === According to shrine tradition, it was established during the reign of the 8th Emperor {{ill|Emperor Kōgen|ja|孝元天皇}}Shrine history.. The earliest record in historical documents is from {{ill|Jogan|ja|貞観}} 8 (866), when it was given the rank of {{ill|Junior Second rank|ja|従二位}} from no rank. Additionally, it is listed as "Takemizuwake Shrine" in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}} compiled in {{ill|Engi|ja|延長}} 5 (927), categorized as a {{ill|Myojin Taisha|ja|名神大}}. However, the evidence supporting the identification of this shrine as the one mentioned in the documents is not definitive『日本の神々』 Takemizuwake Shrine entry., and another candidate is {{ill|Okeno Omi Shrine|ja|桶知大神社}} in Nagano City. The area around Takemizuwake Shrine became an estate ({{ill|Shōen|ja|荘園}}) of {{ill|Iwashimizu Hachiman Shrine|ja|石清水八幡宮}} (Otani estate) from the late Heian period, and it is said that the Hachiman deity (the three deities enshrined together) was invited from Iwashimizu Hachiman Shrine during the Anwa era (968-970). The Hachiman deity is known as the tutelary deity of the {{ill|Minamoto clan|ja|源氏}}, and Takemizuwake Shrine was widely revered by warriors as the foremost Hachiman Shrine in the region. It is also said that {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshinaka|ja|源義仲}} prayed here『参考源平盛衰記』 mentions on June 25 (or 14), Yōwa 1 (1181), that "八幡社ヲ伏拝ミ". However, it is unclear if this "Hachiman Shrine" is the same as Takemizuwake Shrine.. In {{ill|Hōgen|ja|保元}} 3 (1158), there is a record of lands in Otani estate, Sarashina District being confiscated by multiple officials. On that day, a government order was issued to halt thisIwashimizu document. During the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}} (1335), the Four Shrine clan, who served as Shinto priests of Takemizuwake Shrine, together with the Hoshina and Sekiya clans, attacked the {{ill|Shugo|ja|守護所}} (provincial headquarters) in Funeiyama (Suwa), but were suppressed. This resulted in the downfall of the Four Shrine clan, who were said to have served as both {{ill|Jitō|ja|地頭}} and district officials during their peak. The shrine buildings were burned down and later rebuilt at their current location. In {{ill|Tenshō|ja|天正}} 3 (1575), {{ill|Uesugi Kenshin|ja|上杉謙信}} offered a prayer document to the shrine, praying for victory against {{ill|Hōjō Ujizane|ja|北条氏政}}{{ill|Uesugi Kenshin prayer document|ja|上杉謙信願文集}}. In {{ill|Kanei|ja|寛永}} 1 (1624), the Tokugawa shogunate granted 200 koku of shrine land to the shrine. In Meiji 1 (1868), following the separation of Shinto and Buddhism ({{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|ja|神仏分離}}), the shrine was renamed "Takemizuwake Shrine" from "Hachiman Shrine," reflecting the disbanding of the associated temple ({{ill|Shinano Five Mountains|ja|信濃五山}}). Many of the trees are old, and the "Takemizuwake Shrine Grove" is designated as a natural monument by Nagano Prefecture. The grounds, measuring approximately 280 meters from north to south and 70 meters from east to west, were originally square but were eroded into their current rectangular shape by frequent floods from the Chikuma River. A document from the Kanei era (1624-1644) was recently discovered, showing a square layout. Most of the current shrine buildings were constructed after a fire in Tenpō 13 (1842). The main hall was completed in Kaei 3 (1850) by Tatekawa Washiro II from Suwa. The worship hall was completed in Ansei 3 (1856) by Mineura Yagorō under Tatekawa Washiro's supervision. The main hall of the subsidiary Kōra Shrine is the oldest building, having survived the fire. Fourth shrine of {{ill|Shinano Province|ja|信濃国}}
Former {{ill|Prefectural shrine|ja|県社}}
{{ill|Beppyo Shrine|ja|別表神社}} | established = During the reign of the 8th Emperor {{ill|Emperor Kōgen|ja|孝元天皇}} (trad.) | architecture = Nagare-zukuri | nickname = Hachiman Shrine | pilgrimage = | festival = September 15 | rituals = Daitōsai (Niinamesai), December 10-14 | map = Japan Nagano Prefecture | label = Takemizuwake Shrine | relief = 1 | map_width = 256 }} [[File:Takemizuwake-jinja ootorii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{center|Ōtorii}}]] '''Takemizuwake Shrine''' (武水別神社[[ja:武水別神社]]) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Chikuma, Nagano|ja|千曲市}}, Nagano Prefecture, Japan. It is a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} ({{ill|Myojin Taisha|ja|名神大}}) and the fourth shrine of {{ill|Shinano Province|ja|信濃国}}. It was formerly classified as a {{ill|Prefectural shrine|ja|県社}} and is now a {{ill|Beppyo Shrine|ja|別表神社}} under the Association of Shinto Shrines. The shrine's old name was "Hachiman Shrine," and it is still commonly referred to as "Yawata-sama" or "Yawata Shrine." == deity == '''Main deity''' * '''{{ill|Takemizuwake no Ōkami|ja|武美名別命}}''' (Takemizuwake no Ōkami)According to the shrine's history. *: The shrine's tradition states that this deity was enshrined to pray for the fertility of the Zenkoji Plain and to prevent the flooding of the Chikuma River. '''Deities in the Same Shrine''' : The three deities enshrined together here collectively represent the {{ill|Hachiman|lt=Hachiman deity|ja|八幡神}}. * Hondawake no Mikoto (誉田別命, {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|ja|応神天皇}}) * Okinagatarashihime no Mikoto (息長足比売命, {{ill|Empress Jingū|ja|神功皇后}}) * Hime Ōkami (比咩大神) == History == === Overview === According to shrine tradition, it was established during the reign of the 8th Emperor {{ill|Emperor Kōgen|ja|孝元天皇}}Shrine history.. The earliest record in historical documents is from {{ill|Jogan|ja|貞観}} 8 (866), when it was given the rank of {{ill|Junior Second rank|ja|従二位}} from no rank. Additionally, it is listed as "Takemizuwake Shrine" in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}} compiled in {{ill|Engi|ja|延長}} 5 (927), categorized as a {{ill|Myojin Taisha|ja|名神大}}. However, the evidence supporting the identification of this shrine as the one mentioned in the documents is not definitive『日本の神々』 Takemizuwake Shrine entry., and another candidate is {{ill|Okeno Omi Shrine|ja|桶知大神社}} in Nagano City. The area around Takemizuwake Shrine became an estate ({{ill|Shōen|ja|荘園}}) of {{ill|Iwashimizu Hachiman Shrine|ja|石清水八幡宮}} (Otani estate) from the late Heian period, and it is said that the Hachiman deity (the three deities enshrined together) was invited from Iwashimizu Hachiman Shrine during the Anwa era (968-970). The Hachiman deity is known as the tutelary deity of the {{ill|Minamoto clan|ja|源氏}}, and Takemizuwake Shrine was widely revered by warriors as the foremost Hachiman Shrine in the region. It is also said that {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshinaka|ja|源義仲}} prayed here『参考源平盛衰記』 mentions on June 25 (or 14), Yōwa 1 (1181), that "八幡社ヲ伏拝ミ". However, it is unclear if this "Hachiman Shrine" is the same as Takemizuwake Shrine.. In {{ill|Hōgen|ja|保元}} 3 (1158), there is a record of lands in Otani estate, Sarashina District being confiscated by multiple officials. On that day, a government order was issued to halt thisIwashimizu document. During the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|ja|南北朝時代}} (1335), the Four Shrine clan, who served as Shinto priests of Takemizuwake Shrine, together with the Hoshina and Sekiya clans, attacked the {{ill|Shugo|ja|守護所}} (provincial headquarters) in Funeiyama (Suwa), but were suppressed. This resulted in the downfall of the Four Shrine clan, who were said to have served as both {{ill|Jitō|ja|地頭}} and district officials during their peak. The shrine buildings were burned down and later rebuilt at their current location. In {{ill|Tenshō|ja|天正}} 3 (1575), {{ill|Uesugi Kenshin|ja|上杉謙信}} offered a prayer document to the shrine, praying for victory against {{ill|Hōjō Ujizane|ja|北条氏政}}{{ill|Uesugi Kenshin prayer document|ja|上杉謙信願文集}}. In {{ill|Kanei|ja|寛永}} 1 (1624), the Tokugawa shogunate granted 200 koku of shrine land to the shrine. In Meiji 1 (1868), following the separation of Shinto and Buddhism ({{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|ja|神仏分離}}), the shrine was renamed "Takemizuwake Shrine" from "Hachiman Shrine," reflecting the disbanding of the associated temple ({{ill|Shinano Five Mountains|ja|信濃五山}}). The shrine was initially classified as a village shrine ({{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}) in the Modern Shrine ranking System but was promoted to a prefectural shrine ({{ill|Kensha|ja|県社}}) in Meiji 41 (1908). In 1876, the traditional Buddhist ceremony, the Grand Head festival ({{ill|Daitōsai|ja|大頭祭}}), was transformed into a Shinto ritual吉永みち子『もっと馬を!』平凡社、1990年、8 - 20ページ「木曽馬の村」. === Shrine ranks === * Jogan 8 (866) June, promoted from no rank to Junior Second rank (『{{ill|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|ja|日本三代実録}}』) * Jogan 9 (867) March 26, listed as a government shrine (『日本三代実録』) == Shrine Grounds == [[File:Takemizuwake-jinja honden.JPG|thumb|210px|right|{{center|Honden}}]] [[File:Takemizuwake-jinja keidai.JPG|thumb|210px|right|{{center|Shrine Grove (Nagano Prefecture designated natural monument)}}]] The shrine grounds cover 18,896 square meters and include a grove primarily composed of zelkova and cedar trees, with over 20 species and 400 trees in total. Many of the trees are old, and the "Takemizuwake Shrine Grove" is designated as a natural monument by Nagano Prefecture. The grounds, measuring approximately 280 meters from north to south and 70 meters from east to west, were originally square but were eroded into their current rectangular shape by frequent floods from the Chikuma River. A document from the Kanei era (1624-1644) was recently discovered, showing a square layout. Most of the current shrine buildings were constructed after a fire in Tenpō 13 (1842). The main hall was completed in Kaei 3 (1850) by Tatekawa Washiro II from Suwa. The worship hall was completed in Ansei 3 (1856) by Mineura Yagorō under Tatekawa Washiro's supervision. The main hall of the subsidiary Kōra Shrine is the oldest building, having survived the fire. The associated temple, known as Sarashina Hachiman Jinguji, was one of the Shinano Five Mountains of the Tendai sect but was abolished during the Meiji period's anti-Buddhist movement ({{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|ja|廃仏毀釈}}). == Subsidiary Shrines == === Subsidiary Shrines === [[File:Takemizuwake-jinja Kora-sha.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{center|Kōra Shrine}}{{small|The main hall inside the covering structure is a Nagano Prefecture treasure.}}]] * Kōra Shrine (高良社) *: The main hall inside the covering structure is the oldest in the shrine grounds, believed to have been built in the late Muromachi period (16th century). It is designated as a Nagano Prefecture treasureExplanatory panel on-site.. === Associated Shrines === * Emperor Jimmu Shrine * Smallpox Shrine * Sake Brewer Shrine * Yaegaki Shrine * Sukune Shrine * Komagata Shrine * Kojin Shrine * Twelve Shrines * Tenjin Shrine * Koyasu Shrine * Ten stone shrines: Ontake Shrine, Kotohira Shrine, Tōshōgū, Myōgi Shrine, Seki no Kami, Dōsojin, Water God Shrine, Mountain God Shrine, Akiba Shrine, Kashima Shrine == festivals == === festivals === The festivals held at Takemizuwake Shrine are as follows. Particularly notable are the three major festivals: the Prayer festival (March 15), the Grand festival (September 15), and the Grand Head festival (New Harvest festival, December 10-14).

=== Grand Head festival === The Grand Head festival (Niinamesai) held from December 10 to 14 is called the "Daitōsai". The festival is led by five headmen, with the third headman being called "Daitō," giving the festival its name. The "Headman's Record" (御頭帳) traces back to Bunroku 1 (1592), making it a festival with a history of over 400 years. It is designated as an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property of Japan. == Cultural Properties == === Selected Intangible Folk Cultural Property (National Selection) === * Headman's ceremony of Takemizuwake Shrine - Selected on December 17, 1986{{Cultural Property Database|312|353|Headman's ceremony of Takemizuwake Shrine}}. === Nagano Prefecture Designated Cultural Properties === * Nagano Prefecture Treasures (Tangible Cultural Properties) ** main hall of Kōra Shrine (Building) - Muromachi period. Designated on July 21, 1975. ** Bronze Hanging Lantern (Craft) - Muromachi period. Designated on April 13, 1970. * Natural Monument ** Takemizuwake Shrine Grove - Designated on February 25, 1965. * Historic Site ** Takemizuwake Shrine Matsuda House Site - Medieval period.
